Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Discuss relative and absolute indications and contraindications to regional anesthesia.
Describe the major types of regional anesthesia and the application of common nerve blocks.
Explain the major techniques for placement of neuraxial anesthesia, peripheral nerve blocks,
and truncal nerve blocks.
Review the potential complications associated with regional anesthesia.
Overview

Overview




NOTES

Regional anesthesia involves the use of local anesthetic agents and additive medications
to block specific nerves, thereby reducing pain sensation from a large area of the body. It
can be used alone or in combination with general anesthesia or sedation to provide
surgical anesthesia. It also can be used for postoperative analgesia, such as with epidural
patient-controlled analgesia, peripheral nerve catheters, or long-acting single-shot nerve
blocks.
Indications/Advantages

Indications/Advantages
Patients undergoing orthopaedic surgery may present a wide range of anesthetic
challenges because of procedure-specific and patient-specific factors, such as the
elevated risk of thromboembolic events, advanced patient age, and challenges with
postoperative pain control. Orthopaedic procedures often are amenable to regional
anesthesia, which may address many of these challenges. Evidence shows that regional
anesthesia for certain orthopaedic procedures decreases the risk of postoperative
pneumonia, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, systemic infection, and
mortality and decreases transfusion requirements compared with general anesthesia.1-
3In patients with severe cardiovascular, respiratory, or neurologic comorbidities, regional
anesthesia may be a better-tolerated and more hemodynamically stable option for
dense sensory and motor blockade. If used for postoperative pain control, regional
anesthesia is an essential component of multimodal pain management and may be
particularly helpful for chronic pain in patients with high baseline narcotic requirements.
Adequate acute pain control facilitates early ambulation and timely hospital discharge
and increases patient satisfaction.4,5 In addition, an analgesic nerve block, nerve
catheter, or epidural catheter reduces opioid consumption while maintaining adequate
pain relief.6
Contraindications

Contraindications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
2/20

Few absolute contraindications to regional anesthesia exist. The primary
contraindications are patient refusal and infection at the site of injection. Placement of a
block through an infected site increases the risk of systemic infection or infection of a
previously sterile space, such as the epidural space. Allergy to local anesthetic agents
also is an absolute contraindication; however, true allergy to local anesthetic agents is
exceedingly rare, with the incidence being unknown in the general population.7 Several
relative contraindications should be considered, particularly with regard to neuraxial
techniques. Coagulopathy secondary to systemic disease or the use of anticoagulants
result in a prohibitively high risk of bleeding and epidural hematoma formation. Active
systemic infection results in an increased risk of spread to the central nervous system
and the epidural space. Several aortic stenosis or other fixed cardiac output states also
are a relative contraindication to neuraxial anesthesia. Severe spine deformities or the
presence of hardware also may preclude safe spinal or epidural placement. With
peripheral nerve blocks, preexisting neuropathy should be carefully evaluated because
of risk of additional nerve injury.
Types of Regional Anesthesia

Types of Regional Anesthesia
Regional anesthesia can be grossly divided into neuraxial techniques and peripheral
nerve blocks. Selection of a technique is primarily based on the site of surgery; however,
patient anatomy, the duration of analgesia desired, and the ease of participation in
physical therapy may play a role.
Neuraxial Anesthesia

Neuraxial Anesthesia
Neuraxial anesthesia refers to the technique of injecting medication into the epidural or
subarachnoid space. Injection into either location may provide bilateral sensory and
motor blockade of the lower abdomen and extremities. Because of its reliability, rapid
onset, and relative ease of placement, neuraxial anesthesia frequently is used for lower-
extremity orthopaedic surgery. It also has been well studied in the literature, particularly
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
3/20

in the setting of total joint arthroplasty. In patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty,
neuraxial anesthesia reduces transfusion requirements, systemic infection, and
mortality.1,2 It also reduces the risk of several postoperative complications, such as
pneumonia, deep vein thrombosis, and pulmonary embolism compared with general
anesthesia3 (Resource 1).
Combined Spinal Epidural

Combined Spinal Epidural
A combined spinal epidural consists of the placement of an epidural needle via a loss-of-
resistance technique. A spinal needle is then placed through the epidural needle to allow
for subarachnoid injection before being withdrawn, leaving the epidural needle in situ.
An epidural catheter is then threaded through the epidural needle. This technique
provides a rapid onset of motor and sensory block via the spinal dose, whereas the
indwelling catheter allows for prolonged infusion for postoperative analgesia.
Peripheral Nerve Blocks

Peripheral Nerve Blocks
Various peripheral nerve blocks can be performed depending on the desired area of
effect. Each block is performed as a one-time single-shot injection or as a continuous
infusion of local anesthetic through an indwelling catheter. The duration of the block
ranges from several hours to more than 1 day depending on the injectate, which
typically consists of a local anesthetic agent with or without an additive medication, such
dexamethasone, an alpha-2–adrenergic agonist, or buprenorphine.
Upper Extremity
Interscalene Block
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
4/20


Interscalene Block
An interscalene nerve block is the preferred nerve block for proximal humerus and
shoulder surgery. Local anesthetic is deposited at the groove between the anterior and
middle scalene muscles at the level of the cricoid cartilage. This block affords good
coverage of the superior and middle trunks of the branchial plexus but often partially or
completely spares the inferior trunk. If coverage of the ulnar distribution is desired, an
interscalene nerve block may be supplemented with an ulnar nerve block. Because of
the proximity of the phrenic nerve, ipsilateral hemidiaphragm paralysis is almost
universally observed. Horner syndrome and recurrent laryngeal nerve block also may be
present.
Selective Superior Trunk Block

Selective Superior Trunk Block
A selective superior trunk block aims to provide blockade of the superior trunk (C5-6
nerve roots).13 It is a relatively new technique that affords good anesthesia for upper
arm and shoulder surgery. Supplemental blockade of the supraclavicular nerve may be
required for coverage of the cape of the shoulder.14 Compared with an interscalene
nerve block, a selective superior trunk block is associated with a lower risk of phrenic
blockade.
Supraclavicular Block

Supraclavicular Block
A supraclavicular block provides anesthesia from the lower humerus to the hand. For
this block, local anesthetic is deposited above the clavicle at the level of the divisions of
the brachial plexus. It may miss the suprascapular nerve and provide incomplete
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
5/20

coverage of the shoulder. Although a decreased rate of phrenic nerve blockade is
associated with a supraclavicular block compared with an interscalene block,
approximately 35% of patients will experience ipsilateral hemidiaphragm paralysis.15
Proximity of the block needle to the pleura also is associated with a small risk of
pneumothorax (0.4%).16
Infraclavicular Block

Infraclavicular Block
An infraclavicular block commonly is used for coverage of the distal humerus to the
hand. Local anesthetic is deposited below the clavicle at the level of the cords of the
brachial plexus. It is primarily used for elbow, wrist, and hand surgery. Although more
technically challenging than an interscalene or supraclavicular nerve block, an
infraclavicular block avoids hemidiaphragm paralysis and it associated with a low risk of
pneumothorax.
Axillary Block

Axillary Block
An axillary block affords coverage of the elbow, wrist, and hand. It does not cover the
musculocutaneous nerve, which must be supplemented by an additional injection for
some forearm procedures. Despite the relative ease of performing an axillary block, an
infraclavicular block, which may afford a greater area of cover in fewer injections, is
favored.
Digital Block

Digital Block
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
6/20

A digital block can afford anesthesia for minor procedures on the fingers. Two landmark-
based techniques can be used (Resource 2). This block can be performed quickly with
minimal additional equipment.
Lower Extremity
Femoral Block

Femoral Block
A femoral nerve block provides reliable sensory and motor blockade to the anterior
thigh, knee, and medial lower extremity. It is well studied and can be performed without
the use of ultrasonography. Unfortunately, it reliably produces quadriceps weakness,
increasing the risk for falls and decreasing patient ability to participate in physical
therapy.
Adductor Canal Block

Adductor Canal Block
As an alternative to a femoral nerve block, an adductor canal block affords coverage of
the distal thigh, knee, femur, and medial lower extremity with little to no motor
weakness. Dissimilar from a femoral nerve block, an adductor canal block requires
ultrasonographic guidance to deposit local anesthetic into the adductor canal, the walls
of which are formed by the vastus medialis, adductor magnus, and sartorius.
Infiltration Between the Popliteal Artery and Capsule of the Knee Block
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
7/20


Infiltration Between the Popliteal Artery and Capsule of the Knee
Block
This block aims to anesthetize the articular branches to the posterior capsule of the knee
while preserving motor function. It frequently is used in combination with an abductor
canal block to provide analgesia of the knee with minimal motor weakness.
Sciatic Block

Sciatic Block
A sciatic nerve block offers motor and sensory coverage to the posterior aspect of the
upper half of the lower extremity and most of the leg below the knee. Therefore, it is
suitable for most surgical procedures below the knee, provided it is supplemented with a
saphenous nerve block for medial coverage. Multiple approaches have been described
along the course of the sciatic nerve—Labat, popliteal, and subgluteal. It produces a
footdrop, which may mask intraoperative common peroneal nerve injury and impede
early ambulation postoperatively.
Ankle Block

Ankle Block
The ankle block provides adequate anesthesia for foot surgery. It is accomplished via five
separate blocks of the deep peroneal, superficial peroneal, posterior tibial, saphenous,
and sural nerves. All injections can be performed using anatomic landmarks; however,
ultrasonography occasionally is used for supplemental guidance.
Digital Block
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
8/20


Digital Block
A digital block can afford anesthesia for minor toe procedures. This block can be
performed quickly, with minimal additional supplies, via a landmark based technique
(Resource 3).
Trunk
Paravertebral Block

Paravertebral Block
A paravertebral block anesthetizes spinal nerves as they emerge from intervertebral
foramina, resulting in somatic and sympathetic nerve blockade. It is most commonly
used in breast surgery and can afford dense analgesia to the chest wall, similar to an
epidural. Dissimilar from an epidural, a paravertebral block can be used to provide a
unilateral block. It is a technically challenging block that is associated with an increased
risk of pleural puncture and symptomatic pneumothorax. The paravertebral space is a
deep, noncompressible space; therefore, any preexisting coagulopathy should be
carefully considered.
Erector Spinae Plane Block

Erector Spinae Plane Block
An erector spinae plane block consists of local anesthetic deposition deep in the erector
spinae muscle and superficial to the tip of a thoracic transverse process. This affords
coverage of the posterior thorax and abdominal viscera. Data suggest that an erector
spinae plane block can decrease postoperative fentanyl and morphine consumption
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
9/20

after lumbar spine surgery.17,18 The relatively superficial plane of this block enhances its
safety profile because inadvertent pleural or vascular puncture is unlikely.
Spinal Anesthesia

Spinal Anesthesia
Spinal anesthesia is the deposition of local anesthetic potentially opioid medication
directly into the subarachnoid space. It provides rapid onset of dense motor and sensory
blockade about the level of injection and below if using an isobaric local anesthetic,
making it the preferred regional anesthetic technique for orthopaedic procedures from
the waist down to avoid inadvertent injection directly into the spinal cord, spinal
anesthesia is performed only below the level of the conus medullaris (typically L1). The
duration of blockade varies based on the exact local anesthetic used, ranging from less
than 1 hour with the use of chloroprocaine to several hours with bupivacaine. Intrathecal
opioid is less commonly used in orthopaedic surgery but can be added for additional
postoperative pain control. 
Successful spinal placement frequently results in hypotension because of sympathetic
blockade and arterial and venous vasodilation.8 Other adverse effects include nausea
secondary to hypotension, urinary retention from blockade of afferent and efferent
signals to the bladder, and heat loss because of redistribution of blood flow from the
core to the periphery.
Complications of spinal anesthesia in order of decreasing frequency include postdural
puncture headache (PDPH), transient neurologic symptoms, and meningitis. PDPH
commonly presents as positional headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, hypoacusia,
and/or tinnitus within 1 to 3 days.9 It can occur after spinal or inadvertent dural
puncture during epidural placement. Young women in particular have an elevated risk
for PDPH.10 Transient neurologic symptoms represent a self-limited condition of
unknown etiology consisting of pain in the lower extremities or buttocks continuing after
resolution of spinal anesthesia. The condition is associated with the use of spinal
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
10/20

lidocaine and mepivacaine, and symptoms resolve over several days without
management.11 The placement of a spinal anesthetic via poor aseptic technique or in
patients with active systemic infection may increase the risk of meningitis and cause
considerable long-term morbidity.
Epidural Anesthesia

Epidural Anesthesia
Epidural anesthesia differs from spinal anesthesia in that the local anesthetic is
deposited in the epidural space rather than the subarachnoid space. Epidural anesthesia
can provide good sensory and motor blockade but is less dense than a spinal anesthetic
and with slower onset. The advantage of an epidural anesthetic is access to an indwelling
catheter, which allows for redosing for maintenance of surgical block for long
procedures and continuous infusion for management of postoperative pain. Another
advantage of epidural anesthesia is that it can be administered above the level of the
conus medullaris because placement does not violate the dural sac. This allows for
reliable and continuous coverage of higher lumbar and thoracic dermatomes.
Some complications are associated with spinal and epidural anesthesia. Both are
associated with a risk of PDPH; however, the risk is higher with epidural anesthesia than
with spinal anesthesia.11 Epidural anesthesia also is associated with a small risk of
meningitis and epidural abscess from the prolonged presence of an indwelling catheter.
In a study of patients with culture-positive epidural catheters, 14% had meningitis and
2.5% had an epidural abscess.12
Techniques

Techniques
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
11/20

Three primary techniques are used to facilitate peripheral nerve block placement. In
each scenario, the goal is to deposit local anesthetic in close proximity to the selected
nerve without causing inadvertent intravascular injection, nerve trauma, or injury to any
surrounding structures. A combination of techniques can be used to confirm needle
placement and optimize block placement.
Anatomic Landmarks

Anatomic Landmarks
Before the widespread adoption of ultrasonography, anatomic landmarks were the basis
for peripheral nerve block placement. This blind technique is associated with low costs
and requires no additional equipment. Although anatomic landmarks continue to be
used as the primary technique for the placement of certain superficial blocks, they have
largely fallen out of favor because of the increased safety and success rate associated
with blocks performed via ultrasonographic guidance.19-21
Nerve Stimulator

Nerve Stimulator
A nerve stimulator technique relies on anatomic landmarks for initial needle placement
and then uses small electrical impulses to fine-tune needle position. The strength of
electrical current required to elicit a motor response from the target nerve is
proportional to the distance to the nerve. Motor response at very low currents (0.4 mA)
indicates very close proximity to the nerve and possible intraneural placement of the
block needle. Conversely, motor response at high currents (>0.5 mA) suggests
suboptimal needle placement with a considerable distance between the nerve and the
block needle. The stimulation threshold may be altered in patients with preexisting
neuropathy, such as diabetic neuropathy.22
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
12/20

Ultrasonographic Guidance

Ultrasonographic Guidance
Ultrasonographic guidance has been increasingly accepted as the preferred method for
nerve block placement. It affords direct visualization of the target site and the
surrounding anatomy, which substantially increases accuracy and decreases the
incidence of vascular puncture and subsequent local anesthetic toxicity.20,23 It also
allows for real-time visualization of local anesthetic spread on injection, which reduces
the total volume of local anesthetic required. Multiple studies have noted an increase in
the speed of onset of sensory and motor blockade, fewer needle passes, and decreased
time for block completion.23 Evidence showing a decreased rate of nerve injury with
ultrasonographic guidance is lacking; however, the low historical incidence of nerve
injury makes this outcome difficult to investigate. The high relative equipment costs also
may limit availability of ultrasonography in some practice settings.
Risks and Complications
Serious complications resulting from regional anesthesia are rare; however, careful technique
and precautions should be taken to minimize their occurrence.
Local Anesthetic Toxicity

Local Anesthetic Toxicity
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity occurs because of widespread systemic sodium
channel blockade by local anesthetic agents. It is rare, occurring in approximately 0.18%
of patients who receive a peripheral nerve block, with considerable decreases noted
over in past 20 years secondary to increased awareness and improved technique with
ultrasonographic guidance.24 Local anesthetic systematic toxicity may have devastating
effects on the cardiovascular and neurologic systems, leading to mental status changes,
visual changes, seizures, and respiratory compromise. A period of initial sympathetic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
13/20

activation is followed by bradycardia, ventricular arrythmias, cardiovascular collapse,
and death. Although the exact mechanism of action is unclear, lipid recuse therapy is a
mainstay in the management of local anesthetic systemic toxicity. Lipid recuse therapy is
thought to act as a lipid sink that decreases the amount of local anesthetic available to
bind to the patient’s tissues. Other management primarily is supportive and consists of
endotracheal intubation to maintain oxygenation and prevent acidosis, administration of
benzodiazepines to suppress seizures, management of arrythmias and cardiac arrest,
and possible cardiopulmonary bypass.
Nerve Injury

Nerve Injury
Persistent sensory or motor deficits after peripheral nerve blocks are extremely rare.
They are attributed to nerve injury from direct trauma by the block needle, nerve
compression and ischemia from increased local pressure from anesthetic injection, and
neurotoxicity of the local anesthetic or adjuvant medications. Although the exact
definition of injury may vary, approximately 1.8% of patients will have sensory or motor
deficits lasting more than 5 days and 0.9% of patients will have deficits lasting more than
6 months.25 Advanced age, preexisting nerve pathology, and the use of long, beveled
cutting needles appear to be associated with an increased risk of injury; however, many
studies on the mechanics of nerve injury are performed in animals because of ethical
concerns.26
Epidural Hematoma

Epidural Hematoma
Epidural hematoma is a rare complication of neuraxial anesthesia, occurring at a rate of
0.6 per 100,000 individuals.27 It is caused by bleeding into the epidural space and
compresses the spinal cord as a result of vascular puncture, coagulopathy, or traumatic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
14/20

placement of spinal or epidural anesthesia. The cardinal symptoms are progressive
motor and sensory block, and new onset of bowel or bladder dysfunction. Management
consists of emergent neurosurgical decompression.
Block Failure

Block Failure
Block failure may indicate an inability to reach the subarachnoid space during spinal
placement, patchy sensory coverage, or the need for considerable anesthetic
supplementation or full general anesthetic after a peripheral nerve block intended to
serve as the primary anesthetic. Failure rates ranging from 0.5% to 1% for neuraxial
anesthesia are considered possible; however, rates as high as 4% to 17% have been
reported at some teaching institutions.28,29 Peripheral nerve block failure rates vary,
ranging from 0.5% (interscalene block) to 40% (supraclavicular block) among some
trainee populations.14,30 The variable incidence of block failure in the literature reflects
the large degree of heterogeneity in definition and practitioner experience and
technique.
Motor Weakness

Motor Weakness
Motor weakness from neuraxial or peripheral nerve blockade, if limited to the duration
of the local anesthetic, may be unavoidable with certain blocks. Muscle relaxation may
be desirable in some patients to improve surgical conditions; however, its continued
presence postoperatively may hinder early mobility, ability to perform physical therapy,
and rapid discharge from the postanesthesia care unit. Patients also may find the
sensation discomfiting. In these situations, careful nerve block and injectate selection
may aid in minimizing motor weakness. Some blocks can afford dense analgesia with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:58 PM
AAOS | Regional Anesthesia
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002115
15/20

little or no effect on motor function (eg, saphenous nerve block), whereas other blocks
reliably result in at least some degree of weakness (eg, interscalene block).
Mark as Complete
